text: Most people think stroke prevention
looks like taking your medications,
cutting out salt, and avoiding stressful
situations. And don't get me wrong,
those things do matter, but after having
this conversation with patient after
patient, the habits that actually move
the needle and can prevent a stroke from
ever happening in the first place are
almost never the things that people
expect. Because strokes do not happen
randomly. They happen at the end of a
long chain of events that start quietly,
often years before a stroke happens, and
that are highly sensitive to what you do
in just the first hour of every day. The
morning is not just the start of your
day. It's the window where your heart
and blood vessels are most at risk and
most responsive to the right habits. I'm
Dr. Mitch Rice, a practicing
board-certified primary care physician
here in the United States, and today I'm
going to show you seven morning habits
that most people have never heard of
connected to stroke prevention, why the
morning window matters than most people
realize, and exactly how you can start
protecting your brain this week. Before
we get into the habits, I want to fully
explain why the morning is such a
critical window. Most strokes do not
happen randomly throughout the day. The
vast majority of strokes happen early in
the morning, specifically between the
hours of 5:00 a.m. and 12:00 p.m. And
the reason is simple biology. When you
wake up, three things happen all at
once. Your main stress hormone spikes to
its highest point of the day, your blood
gets a little thicker and stickier after
hours without water, and your blood
pressure shoots up sharply, sometimes
dramatically, in the first hour after
waking. This is normal and called the
morning blood pressure surge, and it's
one of the strongest predictors of
stroke risk in all of medicine, and
almost nobody is doing anything
specifically to manage it. Now, let me
walk you through each of these seven
things that you can start doing this
week, and I I you to pay super close
attention to numbers three and six on
this list because those are the ones
that will genuinely shock you. Habit
number one is to drink water before
anything else. After 7 to 8 hours
without fluid, your blood is slightly
thicker than at any other point in the
day. Thick blood will move slowly. It's
harder for your heart to push through
the vessels and it's far more likely for
clots to form, which is the direct cause
of the most common type of stroke.
Research published in the European
Journal of Nutrition found that drinking
water in the morning measurably reduced
blood thickness and stickiness, two of
the main clotting drivers behind stroke.
Drink roughly 500 ml or about 16 oz of
water before coffee, before food, and
before you do anything else. Room
temperature or cold water both work and
this one habit honestly takes about 2 to
3 minutes and can start protecting you
right away. Habit number two is to get
into some morning sunlight within the
first 10 minutes of being awake. Most
people think that morning sunlight only
affects your mood, but the connection to
stroke runs a bit deeper. Natural light
hitting your eyes within the first 10
minutes of waking sends a signal to a
small but powerful part of your brain,
your body's master clock. When that
signal fires correctly, your stress
hormone peaks, does its job, and starts
falling within 45 minutes. But when that
signal is missing because you woke up in
a dark room and went straight to your
phone, that stress hormone stays high
and messy all day. And when your stress
hormone stay elevated all day, it raises
blood pressure, causes inflammation in
your blood vessels, and makes your blood
stickier. All three of those things
directly increase stroke risk over time.
You want to step outside within 10
minutes of being awake. Even on cloudy
days, outdoor light is far brighter than
indoor lighting. Two to five minutes is
enough to trigger this response. And try
not to wear sunglasses as the light
needs to reach your eyes directly to be
most effective. Habit number three is
the one that most people have never
heard of in terms of it directly
connecting the increased risk of having
a stroke, and that is to breathe only
through your nose during morning
movement. Whether you walk, stretch, or
do any kind of morning movement, how you
breathe during that movement has a
direct effect on your stroke risk.
Breathing through your nose produces a
molecule called nitric oxide inside your
sinuses with every breath. That nitric
oxide travels directly into your
bloodstream, and nitric oxide tells your
blood vessel walls to relax and open up,
which lowers blood pressure at the exact
moment of the day when it's at its most
dangerous peak. Breathing through your
mouth produces almost none of this.
Research found that nose-only breathing
during exercise produced significantly
lower blood pressure compared to mouth
breathing at the exact same workout
intensity. So, during your morning walk
or movement, keep your mouth closed.
Slow down if needed. Nasal breathing
gets easier within 2 to 3 weeks of
practice. And even just 5 minutes of
nose breathing during movement produces
real benefits. Habit number four is to
eat your protein first before any
carbohydrates at breakfast. Now, the
order in which you eat your breakfast
matters just as much as what you eat for
breakfast. When you eat carbohydrates
first, like toast or cereal, your blood
sugar spikes rapidly. That fast rise
causes a big wave of insulin to flood
your system. And insulin turns up your
fight-or-flight response, that same
response that's already running high in
the morning because of the natural blood
pressure surge. Stacking an insulin wave
on top of an already stressed morning
cardiovascular system is something I see
constantly in patients with poorly
controlled morning blood pressure.
Research published in the Journal of
Diabetes Care found that eating protein
before carbohydrates at the same meal
reduced post-meal insulin spikes by up
to 57%. Less insulin means less
fight-or-flight response, which means
lower blood pressure in the morning. And
a lower blood pressure peak directly
reduces stroke risk during the most
dangerous window of the day. Try to
start every breakfast with protein,
either eggs, Greek yogurt, salmon, or
cottage cheese, and eat at least half
your protein before touching
carbohydrates. This usually looks like
eating about 5 to 10 bites of protein
before going for the carbs. Habit number
five has some of the strongest direct
stroke prevention evidence on this
entire list. It's almost something that
nobody makes sense of, and that is to
eat a nitrate-rich
food at breakfast. Certain vegetables
like beets, arugula, and spinach are
packed with compounds called dietary
nitrates. When you eat these foods, your
bodies turn those nitrates into nitric
oxide. Nitric oxide is the same molecule
that's produced with nasal breathing,
but dietary nitrates work through a
completely different pathway, and they
keep working for hours after you eat. A
major study found that people with
higher dietary nitrate intake had a 17%
lower risk of stroke compared to those
who ate the least. And there have been
multiple studies that have shown that
eating beets or drinking beetroot juice
can directly lower blood pressure for
about 1 to 2 hours after consumption.
What you want to do is to add a handful
of arugula or spinach or beets at
breakfast. You can also try to drink a
small glass of beetroot juice in the
morning, as this is available at most
grocery stores. Try not to use
antibacterial mouthwash before eating,
as this kills the bacteria in your mouth
that converts nitrates into nitric
oxide. Habit number six is 5 minutes of
slow and intentional breathing before
leaving your house in the morning. Most
people think that slow breathing can
help with stress, and while that is
true, it also can help reduce the risk
of having a stroke. The key to breathing
in a calm, controlled way is to make
your exhalation longer than your
inhalation. When your exhale is longer
than your inhale, your heart rate slows,
your blood pressure drops, and your
blood vessels relax. 5 minutes of this
before the day changes something called
heart rate variability in a way that
lasts for hours. Heart rate variability
is the tiny difference in between each
of your heartbeats. When heart rate
variability is low, your stroke risk
goes up. But when heart rate variability
is high, the heart and blood vessels are
working efficiently and flexibly.
Research published in the Journal of
Cell Reports Medicine found that just
five minutes of this kind of breathing
every day produced meaningful
improvements in heart rate variability
within four weeks. What you want to do
is to breathe in through your nose for
about four seconds and then breathe out
slowly through your mouth for six to
eight seconds. Do this for five minutes
before leaving your home. You can do it
outside in the morning sunlight to stack
these two habits at once. Habit number
seven is something that you can actually
track over time, and that is to check
your blood pressure after about 20
minutes of being awake in the morning.
This feels passive, but honestly, it's
not. A single blood pressure reading at
your doctor's office at 2:00 p.m. tells
you almost nothing about the most
dangerous window of your day and what
your blood pressure is doing at your
normal baseline. Research published in
the Journal of Hypertension found that
morning blood pressure surge predicted
stroke risk even in patients whose
clinic blood pressure looked completely
normal. Knowing your morning number is
not scary, it can actually be
protective. And it's the difference
between catching a dangerous pattern at
home early enough to fix it and finding
out about it too late. So, you want to
try to check your blood pressure within
the first 20 minutes of being awake
before medication and before coffee.
Now, you don't need to do all seven
things at once, but start with one or
two habits and try them out for about
four weeks. After you've mastered those
habits, then layer the next one one by
